title: Glassiness and dynamic arrest in magnetic and non-magnetic colloids
authors: Anuj Kumar Singh, Lambert Münster, Martin Weigel, Varsha Banerjee
abstract: We investigate and compare a range of indicators for glassiness in monodisperse magnetic and non-magnetic soft-sphere fluids at low temperatures with a view to exploring the effect of the magnetic moment. We perform extensive molecular dynamics simulations using the Stockmayer model for magnetic fluids and a pure Lennard-Jones interaction for the non-magnetic case. Our investigations involve quenching experiments, in which both systems are rapidly cooled deep below their freezing temperatures. Although the Lennard-Jones fluid forms compact aggregates, the inclusion of dipolar interactions promotes the development of branched and open morphologies. After characterizing the static properties of the frozen structures, we focus on their dynamics. A key observable is the self-part of the van Hove function, which measures the probability that a particle is displaced by a distance $Δ$ over time $t$. In both fluids, this function exhibits non-Gaussian behavior --- thereby providing a signature of dynamic heterogeneity and glassiness. This behavior stems from a separation of time scales between two distinct processes: mobile particles that escape their environments and immobile particles that vibrate within cages. In particular, we find a heavier tail in the van Hove function for the Stockmayer fluid, which is a consequence of the strongly correlated motion in chain-like structures found there. These findings shed light on core relaxation mechanisms in magnetic fluids, advancing our understanding of magnetically responsive colloidal systems.
summary: This work uses molecular dynamics simulations to study glassiness in magnetic and non-magnetic colloidal fluids. By analyzing the van Hove function and employing the CTRW model, the authors quantify how magnetic dipole interactions promote specific structural arrangements and modify the underlying slow dynamics compared to simple LJ systems. The findings advance the understanding of relaxation mechanisms in magnetically responsive soft matter.
main_problem: The study investigates and compares various indicators for glassiness and dynamic arrest in both magnetic and non-magnetic soft-sphere fluids, specifically quantifying the influence of magnetic moments.
main_result: The inclusion of dipolar interactions leads to branched, open morphologies and a heavier tail in the van Hove function compared to non-magnetic systems, indicating strongly correlated motion and modified relaxation mechanisms.
method: The research employs extensive Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations, analyzing dynamics through the self-part of the van Hove function and fitting the data using the Continuous Time Random Walk (CTRW) formalism.
model_or_system: The system consists of monodisperse soft-sphere fluids simulated using either a pure Lennard-Jones (LJ) interaction (non-magnetic) or the Stockmayer model (SM) which includes anisotropic dipolar interactions. The simulations involve rapid quenching deep below freezing temperatures.
key_observables: Self-part of the van Hove function, Non-Gaussianity Parameter ($\alpha(t)$), Edwards-Anderson (EA) parameter ($q_{EA}$), Softness Order Parameter ($S_i$), and the Magnetization ($M$).
important_parameters: Low temperatures, deep quenches, dipole strength ($\mu$), and the exponents $t_1$ and $t_2$ derived from the CTRW fit.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on separating the total van Hove function into contributions from vibrational motion and particle jumps within the M-CTRM formalism, though the authors note this separation may be imperfect.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the fitting parameters ($l, d, t_1, t_2$) and the resulting van Hove function for both LJ and SM fluids, comparing the quantitative results derived from the CTRW model.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the physical models (LJ vs. SM), then characterizing static properties and dynamics using multiple observables ($g(r), q_{EA}, S_i$), and finally applying the advanced M-CTRM formalism to fit the time-dependent van Hove function.
why_interesting: The detailed analysis of dynamic heterogeneity using advanced statistical mechanics tools like the van Hove function and CTRW formalism provides a quantitative framework for understanding how long-range, anisotropic interactions (like dipoles) fundamentally alter the relaxation pathways in glassy materials.

Representative morphologies at density ρ = 0.3 are shown for the SM fluid at temperature T = 0.4 in (b) and for the LJ fluid at T = 0.1 in (d). Corresponding xz-slices are provided in (c) and (e) to enhance visualization. Additionally, a prototypical SM particle is also displayed for clarity.

Data are averaged over 10, 40, and 5 independent samples for N = 1000, N = 2000, and N = 5000, respectively.

The bottom row shows prototypical xz-slices for the SM fluid, corresponding to the configuration shown in Fig. 1(b). The particles are color-coded as per (d) NN, (e) Si, and (f) ∆, with color bars in the panels.
